title: DIAGNOSTIC ALGORITHM AND TREATMENT FOR MICROSCOPIC COLITIS: A REVIEW.

subsections.subsection_title: Definition, Clinical Significance, and Disease Spectrum
subsections.content: recent population-based studies is found in ~10-15% of patients with chronic watery diarrhea undergoing endoscopy with multiply biopsy ref [1], ref [2].MC is a benign condition that has been shown to severely impact health-related quality of life (HRQOL), with baseline HRQOL being lower than that of patients with ulcerative colitis, anal fissures, chronic constipation and faecal incontinence.The natural history of MC varies considerably ref [1], ref [3].Many cases are self-limiting, with symptoms lasting a few weeks or months and resolution of diarrhea in up to 50% of patients receiving steroid treatment ref [1].Unlike other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), there is no evidence that the persistence of histological inflammation predicts long-term negative outcomes such as colorectal cancer or need for surgery ref [1], ref [2].

It is important to emphasize that the aim of this review is to focus on the diagnostic tools that should improve our clinical practice and treatment algorithm of a patients with microscopic colitis. From a population-based study and a nationwide cohort study, microscopic colitis is an important clinical entity with a measurable population burden, with incidence increasing with age and being associated with female sex, and with reported incidence around 21.0 to 24.7 cases per 100,000 person-years in recent cohorts ref [4] ref [5]. From present epidemiologic literature, it also appears that increasing diagnostic activity, including more colon biopsies, may partly contribute to rising detected case numbers in some settings ref [5].

Usually colonoscopy cannot be avoided in patients with chronic diarrhea, and the population burden of microscopic colitis supports maintaining a low threshold for diagnostic evaluation, especially in older women in whom incidence is highest ref [4] ref [5].

Two histological subtypes have been described: Collagenous colitis (CC) and Lymphocytic colitis (LC) ref [6].The clinical symptoms and clinical findings do not differ between MC subgroups.LC is defined by an increased number of surface intraepithelial lymphocytes ref [6].The key histological feature for CC is defined by a thickened collagen band underneath the surface epithelium ref [6].Incomplete and variant forms showing less characteristic features and they also have been reported under different names ref [6].It is also raising suspicions that the two conditions are two histological manifestations of the same entity, possibly representing different manifestations during the disease course or different stages of disease development ref [6].Presently, these entities are considered variants of the same condition.

The natural history of MC varies considerably.Many cases are self-limiting, with symptoms lasting a few weeks or months.Unlike other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), there is no evidence that the persistence of histological inflammation predicts long-term negative outcomes such as colorectal cancer or need for surgery.

The temporal evolution of histological abnormalities shows that pathological changes of CC and LC are more persistent than those of incomplete MC, and that a minority of patients may change to a different MC subgroup over time ref [7].Pre-diagnostic biopsies may already reveal increased lamina propria inflammation before full diagnostic criteria for MC are met ref [7].

subsections.subsection_title: Etiology, Risk Factors, and Associated Conditions
subsections.content:
recent population-based studies is found in ~10-15% of patients with chronic watery diarrhea undergoing endoscopy with multiply biopsy. MC is a benign condition that has been shown to severely impact health-related quality of life (HRQOL), with baseline HRQOL being lower than that of patients with ulcerative colitis, anal fissures, chronic constipation and faecal incontinence. The natural history of MC varies considerably. Many cases are self-limiting, with symptoms lasting a few weeks or months and resolution of diarrhea in up to 50% of patients receiving steroid treatment. Unlike other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), there is no evidence that the persistence of histological inflammation predicts long-term negative outcomes such as colorectal cancer or need for surgery.

Two histological subtypes have been described: Collagenous colitis (CC) and Lymphocytic colitis (LC). The clinical symptoms and clinical findings do not differ between MC subgroups. LC is defined by an increased number of surface intraepithelial lymphocytes. The key histological feature for CC is defined by a thickened collagen band underneath the surface epithelium. Incomplete and variant forms showing less characteristic features and they also have been reported under different names. It is also raising suspicions that the two conditions are two histological manifestations of the same entity, possibly representing different manifestations during the disease course or different stages of disease development. Presently, these entities are considered variants of the same condition.

For many authors, MC is an inflammatory disease of the intestine and thus it is regarded as being a new member of the group of IBD. The etiology of MC is unknown, and studies to solve disease pathogenesis are still in their beginning. The pathophysiology of MC is still unknown, but there is strong evidence that MC is frequently associated with the use of certain medications and certain systemic disorders (such as autoimmune diseases). It is consider that MC is a multifactorial disease, probably secondary to an abnormal immune reaction that appears in predisposed individuals, triggered by different luminal factors (infections, drugs, autoimmunity and/or bile acids), with subsequent epithelial barrier dysfunction in the colonic mucosa. The potential pathophysiological mechanism by which the alteration of the mucosal immune response generates the dominant symptom of the disease (diarrhea) is still under investigation, with several data showing that the diarrhea in MC patients could have an inflammatory origin. Recent studies have revealed that MC is an immune-mediated disorder, with a prominent contribution from the adaptive immune system and cytotoxic responses. Another supporting hypothesis of an immune-mediated cause of MC is the close association of MC with celiac disease, thyroid disease, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome and Raynaud's syndrome ref [4]. In some study reports, celiac disease has been reported to be associated with LC between 4% to 31% of patients with celiac disease and also exhibit histopathological changes typical of LC.

A variety of drugs have been associated with MC and are supposed to induce MC. The increased use of medications, especially in older people, and this might explain the reported increased incidence of MC worldwide. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), statins, topiramate, venotonic agents and histamine antagonists have been associated with MC ref [10]. In fact, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear ref [10]. Current exposure to NSAIDs, PPIs or SSRIs and prolonged use for 4-12 months increased the risk of developing MC ref [10]. Genetic factors or the involvement of miRNAs have been suggested, but they remain largely controversial. Research has also explored genetic associations, with a recent genome-wide association study finding several loci that were associated with CC, including some that have been associated with IBD ref [8]. The genetic associations are poorly understood, and we are still far from being able to outline a possibly complex genetic risk profile for the diagnosis of MC. Bile acid malabsorption (BAM) can coexists with MC, leading to more frequent bowel movements and looser stool consistency. A systemic analysis and some small retrospective case series that have found BAM to be presented in up to 60 % of patients with LC and in up to 44 % of those with CC, supporting the notion that BAM might have a key role in the development of the MC.

It is important to emphasize that the aim of this review is to focus on the diagnostic tools that should improve our clinical practice and treatment algorithm of a patients with microscopic colitis. From a systematic review and meta-analysis on the diagnostic overlap between functional bowel disorders and MC shows that there is a significant overlap of symptoms between MC and IBS-D. This data suggests that ruling out a diagnosis of MC by means of colonoscopy and adequate mucosal biopsies should always be considered, especially in patients with IBS-D. The differential diagnosis of MC is very large and mainly includes infectious colitis, resolving acute infectious colitis, post-dysenteric IBS, drug-induced changes, particularly those related to the intake of non-steroidal inflammatory drugs, but the classic IBD and celiac disease also have to be ruled out. Usually colonoscopy cannot be avoided in patients with chronic diarrhea, but the ability to identify a subset of patients at higher risk of MC has the potential to reduce the number of patients in whom biopsies are taken and recent scoring systems have been proposed to identify lower risk patients. From present literature it has to be assumed that there is an emerging need to identify a non-invasive diagnostic tool that can predict the presence of active MC and distinguish MC from other functional and organic causes of watery diarrhea.

subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Diagnostic Approach and Differential Diagnosis
subsections.content:
Despite frequent diarrhoea, laboratory tests are usually normal or disclose unspecific abnormalities ref [14] ref [16].Until this moment, no reliable serum marker has been identified in MC ref [16].The common serological inflammatory marker, such as C-Reactive Protein is usually normal or only slightly elevated in MC ref [14].However, the prevalence of antinuclear antibodies, anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae IgG antibodies, anti-thyroid peroxidase, anti-perinuclear neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase was significantly higher compared to controls ref [14].

Upon endoscopic evaluation, the mucosa is normal in the vast majority of cases, but may occasionally show subtle changes, such as oedema and erythema ref [14] ref [16].Endoscopic appearance of the colon of MC patients may vary between patients, and may not always appear as a macroscopically normal mucosa ref [16]. A warning about these finding is that they may also appear in non-MC cases, and therefore the disease sensitivity is not guaranteed ref [16].When using advanced endoscopic imaging techniques such as narrow band imaging (NBI) or Fujinon Intelligence Color Enhancement (FICE) may further reveal MC-related or MC-specific endoscopic findings ref [16].There are limited data on the use of indigo carmine to identify endoscopic changes in MC. Vital staining in this situation may allow targeted biopsies. There are also reports of real-time diagnosis using confocal microscopy. This modality holds promise, but the current costs of fixed and disposable components make it more of a research tool at this point. In one study was investigated the endoscopic features of MC with high-definition (HD+) endoscopy plus i-scan. The research team found in 6 patients with MC mosaic pattern/celiaclike mucosa in 2/2 of the CC and 2/4 of the LC. Dwindling or deranged vascular pattern and blotchy erythema were visible in 2/2 of CC and 2/4 of LC. Friability or exudative bleeding and scars or -cat-scratch‖ appearance of the mucosa were present in 1/2 and 1/4 of CC and LC respectively. Furthermore, due to the frequent patchy distribution of such lesions, HD+ endoscopy plus i-scan may help to guide targeted biopsies thus reducing the false negative rate. The importance of endoscopic survey in the diagnosis of MC is also emphasized in taking biopsies from each part of the colonic segment ref [14] ref [16].It is highly recommended to take at least two biopsies per segment, to assure a high likelihood of detecting any present MC-specific pathological findings ref [14] ref [16].However, tangential sectioning of the biopsy specimen can mimic a thickened collagen band, and finally a slightly increased subepithelial collagen band can be found in hyperplastic polyps ref [14].

No pathological microorganisms are generally found in microbiological stool analyses in patients with MC. In MC imaging with radiology is usually normal. The quantification of inflammatory parameters in stool is considered specific for intestinal inflammation, and there have been several attempts to identify a fecal biomarker of inflammation in MC to aid the pre-diagnostic screening and subsequent monitoring of MC. Fecal biomarkers evaluated in MC include a heterogeneous group of substances or proteins that either leak from or are generated by the inflamed mucosa in the gut. The fecal markers can be good supportive tools for the diagnosis of MC. The neutrophilderived proteins calprotectin and myeloperoxidase (MPO) detected in feces have emerged as markers of intestinal inflammation in patients with ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, and their elevated levels correlate with disease activity. On the other hand, despite being primarily expressed by inflammatory cells, such as neutrophilic granulocytes, these biomarkers do not reflect the lymphocytic mucosal infiltration and their diagnostic accuracy is usually low in patients with MC ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Fecal Biomarkers for Detection and Disease Activity
subsections.content: Calprotectin, also known as S100A8/S100A9 complex, is a calcium-binding protein with antibacterial, antiproliferative and immunomodulating effects (Donato et al. 2013).It constitutes two-third of the cytosolic proteins stored into neutrophilic granulocytes (Donato et al. 2013).In large cohorts fecal calprotectin (FC) was significantly increased compared to healthy controls and decreased significantly when remission was induced in MC (ref [17], ref [18]).

subsections.subsection_title: Emerging Molecular and Neuroendocrine Diagnostic Markers
subsections.content: In one study is demonstrated that the mucosal inflammation in active CC is characterized by eosinophil activation in addition to the lymphocytic infiltration of the epithelium and the lamina propria.The eosinophil is regarded as a potent proinflammatory cell with the ability to release cytotoxic proteins such as eosinophil protein X (EPX) and eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), both detectable in blood and feces.In a pilot study of 12 patients with active CC, fecal EPX and fecal ECP were positive in 67% and 92%, respectively, and both markers decreased after budesonide treatment.Given this information, eosinophil markers of inflammation seem to be the most promising tool to detect patients with active CC.In very recent study, Wagner et al. tested the diagnostic performance of fecal ECP and EPX, together with FC and fecal MPO, in a cohort of 67 patients referred to colonoscopy due to chronic non-bloody diarrhea.The results demonstrate that elevated fecal EPX and fecal ECP can predict a diagnostic outcome of CC in patients with chronic non-bloody diarrhea.This specific setting is very important, since it summarize the clinical scenario where the availability of MC biomarkers could represent a step forward in clinical practice.According to endoscopy and pathology reports (available for 63 out of 67 patients), 46 patients were affected with IBS, 2 with UC, 2 with Crohn's disease, 2 with LC, and 9 with CC.Notably, fecal ECP and EPX were significantly higher in CC patients and when all the four tested fecal markers (ECP, EPX, FC, and MPO) were negative, the chances of getting a normal histological description were 92%.Additionally, in the same study, serum levels of ECP and EPX were also measured, without finding any differences between the different study groups.Therefore, it is possible to use the EPX and ECP as diagnostic markers for CC.In contrast, the mucosal inflammation in LC is dominated by an infiltration of lymphocytes.In line with this, fecal EPX and fecal ECP levels did not predict a diagnosis of LC in their study.This finding should, however, be interpreted with caution because of the small number of patients with LC (n-4).Also interesting in this study is that only three out of 13 patients with MC displayed elevated levels of FC.It should be noted that FC is not unique to the neutrophil.Fecal eosinophil-derived proteins may be able to distinguish collagenous from lymphocytic colitis or other causes of diarrhea, but these studies are small and further work is necessary to validate the role of fecal markers of inflammation in the diagnosis and monitoring of MC. In addition, fecal neuroendocrine markers including chromogranin A, chromogranin B, and secretoneurin have been reported to be increased in collagenous colitis, with fecal secretoneurin decreasing to control levels during treatment, suggesting potential value as emerging molecular and neuroendocrine markers in CC ref [2].

subsections.subsection_title: Inflammatory Cell Activity as a Diagnostic Correlate
subsections.content:
Other markers:-Other markers such as chromogranin A, chromogranin B, or secretoneurin are suggested to be a candidate fecal marker for CC.A research group reported increased levels of fecal neuropeptides, suggesting involvement of the enteric nervous system in the pathogenesis of CC.Levels of chromogranin A, chromogranin B, and secretoneurin were increased in 12 patients with CC compared both to controls and patients with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease.During budesonide therapy, levels of secretoneurin rapidly declined.These early data require further study and confirmation in bigger patient cohorts before they may be applied as potential biomarkers in MC.Chromogranin A is therefore considered to be a general marker for all endocrine cells.Colonic chromogranin Apositive cell density being proposed as a diagnostic marker for LC.

From pathophysiological perspective, these findings indicate that activation of both eosinophilic, neutrophilic leucocytes and macrophages might play a role in pathophysiology in patients with MC ref [20].In conclusion, studies researching fecal markers in MC are small and the potential role of fecal markers as a prediagnostic screening or monitoring in patients with known MC deserves further study.

subsections.subsection_title: Histopathological Subtypes and Core Diagnostic Features
subsections.content:
The pathologic evaluation of the biopsy specimens is the most important part of the diagnosis of MC ref [13]. Whether a patient may be diagnosed as CC or LC completely depends on the existence of the specific pathological findings in the biopsy specimens ref [6].

The key histological feature of collagenous colitis is a broad, thickened collagen band under the surface epithelium ref [6]. The band does not usually extend around the crypts, and is most evident between the crypts immediately beneath the surface epithelial cells ref [6]. According to the ECCO-ESP, the thickness of the collagen band should exceed 10 μm (normal <3 μm) in well-oriented biopsies, i.e. biopsies cut perpendicularly to the mucosal surface ref [6].

5.1 It is of big importance to obtain precise and complete clinical information regarding the drugs that may cause symptoms of diarrhea or cause inflammatory changes, since several drugs (e.g., PPI, NSAIDs) may cause histological features of MC, and both the clinical and histological pictures may reverse following drug withdrawal ref [6]. 5.2 Sampling of the colonic mucosa, with at the very least two biopsies from any segment of the colon including the terminal ileum, and correctly oriented samples (on acetate cellulose filters if possible) is needed for a correct histological evaluation, to avoid sampling bias due to too few biopsies and distortion of the fixed samples that may impair a precise evaluation by the pathologist ref [6]. 5.3 Diagnosed should be made on the basis of strict histological criteria ref [6]. Therefore, it is important to use CD3 to count IELs in the superficial epithelium for LC and the trichrome stain to evaluate the collagen band for CC ref [6]. It is worth noting that this band may be intermittently present in the colon ref [6]. 5.4 Apart from the variant forms displaying precise morphological characteristics, such as pseudomembranous collagenous colitis and cryptic lymphocytic colitis, authors suggest avoiding terms such as MCi and -undefined‖ microscopic colitis (UMC) in daily practice, because these terms are misleading and contradictory, with the result that other conditions such as infective, ischemic, pseudomembranous colitis, segmental colitis related to diverticular disease, and inflammatory bowel diseases may be underdiagnosed ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Practical Diagnostic Workflow and Clinicopathologic Correlation
subsections.content:
The characteristic finding on biopsy in lymphocytic colitis is intraepithelial lymphocytosis, defined as >20 intraepithelial lymphocytes (IEL) per 100 surface epithelial cells, with little or no crypt architectural distortion has been adopted in the European Consensus on the Histopathology of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (ECCO-ESP) ref [16].

 Thickening (>10 μm) of the subepithelial collagen band (most prominent in the right colon; rectosigmoid may be normal)  Marked surface epithelial injury (flattening, detachment)  Increased (and homogeneously distributed) mononuclear inflammation in the lamina propria (lymphocytes and plasma cells)  No or little crypt architectural distortion  An increased number of surface intraepithelial lymphocytes (<20 per 100 epithelial cells) may be present  Focal inflammatory bowel disease-like changes (cryptitis and Paneth cell metaplasia) possible  Technical note: H&E-stained slides are generally sufficient to make the diagnosis; collagen stains or tenascin immunostaining may highlight the thickened collagen band, but are not needed routinely ref [16].In borderline cases, additional collagen-specific stains should be used for better visualization (Goldner, van Gieson, Masson-Trichrome) or immunohistochemistry with antibodies directed against tenascin may be helpful ref [16].A direct relationship between the thickness of the collagen band and the clinical symptoms does not seem to exist ref [21].

subsections.subsection_title: Emerging Biomarkers and Their Diagnostic Limitations
subsections.content:
 An increased number of surface intraepithelial lymphocytes (>20 per 100 epithelial cells). Mild surface epithelial injury (vacuolization, flattening, and mucin depletion)  Increased (and homogeneously distributed) mononuclear inflammation in the lamina propria (lymphocytes and plasma cells)  No or little crypt architectural distortion  Thickening (<10 μm) of the subepithelial collagen band may be present  Focal inflammatory bowel disease-like changes (cryptitis and Paneth cell metaplasia) possible  Technical note: H&E-stained slides are generally sufficient to make the diagnosis; CD3 immunostaining may highlight intraepithelial lymphocytes, but is not needed routinely ref [17].

Recently the term incomplete microscopic colitis (MCi) was introduced, for patients with diarrhea and an increase of cellular infiltrates that do not fulfill the histological criteria of CC or LC ref [17].In these cases with MCi patients, an increase in the number of IELs is observed, but <20/100 epithelial cells in superficial epithelium (incomplete LC) and abnormal thickening of the subepithelial collagen band <10 μm (incomplete CC) ref [17].Some patients meeting these criteria have been shown to respond to treatment for MC suggesting that these definitions are appropriate, but more research is required to ascertain if these broadened definitions should be accepted ref [17].

The first step in managing patients with MC is to look for factors that might be exacerbating diarrhea, such as consumption of dairy products in a patient with lactose intolerance or excessive use of artificial sweeteners ref [11]. It is required to make a review of the patient's medication list, including over-the-counter products, to identify drugs or other substances that might cause MC or worsen diarrhea (Table 1) ref [11]. As the pathogenesis of the disease remains unclear, the goal of treatment in MC is to achieve clinical remission, that is <3 stools a day or <1 watery stool a day with subsequent improve quality of life ref [11]. Currently, there are no evidences to consider histological remission as an aim in the treatment of MC ref [11]. Before starting medical treatment, the discontinuation of those drugs that could induce MC should be proposed ref [11].

The goals of treatment are the same as any chronic inflammatory systemic disease: induction of remission, and once achieved, maintenance of remission (be it with expectant management or formal pharmacotherapy) ref [12].There are several treatment options available for patients with MC (Figure 1).However, budesonide is the only option that has been well studied in controlled clinical trials and is currently recommended by the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) as first-line therapy ref [12].Mesalazine is a bowel-specific anti-inflammatory agent, structurally related to the salicylates, that is active in IBD.In patients with symptomatic MC in whom budesonide therapy is not feasible, the AGA suggests treatment with mesalazine over no treatment for the induction of clinical remission ref [12].Because of the uncertain balance between benefits and potential harms, mesalazine is recommended conditionally as a potential second-line therapy that can be used under select circumstances ref [12].Moderate-quality evidence from a single RCT suggests that mesalazine therapy is associated with a lower likelihood of achieving clinical response when compared with no treatment ref [12].

. There are no RCT comparing efficacy of anti-diarrheals against placebo or other medical therapy for MC. Some authors think that anti-diarrheals may be used alone in mild MC or in conjunction with other therapies in moderate to severe MC to reduce frequency of diarrhea ref [22].

subsections.subsection_title: Dietary and Lifestyle Considerations in Management
subsections.content:
The first step in managing patients with MC is to look for factors that might be exacerbating diarrhea, such as consumption of dairy products in a patient with lactose intolerance or excessive use of artificial sweeteners.It is required to make a review of the patient's medication list, including over-the-counter products, to identify drugs or other substances that might cause MC or worsen diarrhea (Table 1).As the pathogenesis of the disease remains unclear, the goal of treatment in MC is to achieve clinical remission, that is <3 stools a day or <1 watery stool a day with subsequent improve quality of life.Currently, there are no evidences to consider histological remission as an aim in the treatment of MC.Before starting medical treatment, the discontinuation of those drugs that could induce MC should be proposed.

The goals of treatment are the same as any chronic inflammatory systemic disease: induction of remission, and once achieved, maintenance of remission (be it with expectant management or formal pharmacotherapy).There are several treatment options available for patients with MC (Figure 1).However, budesonide is the only option that has been well studied in controlled clinical trials and is currently recommended by the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) as first-line therapy.Mesalazine is a bowel-specific anti-inflammatory agent, structurally related to the salicylates, that is active in IBD.In patients with symptomatic MC in whom budesonide therapy is not feasible, the AGA suggests treatment with mesalazine over no treatment for the induction of clinical remission.Because of the uncertain balance between benefits and potential harms, mesalazine is recommended conditionally as a potential second-line therapy that can be used under select circumstances.Moderate-quality evidence from a single RCT suggests that mesalazine therapy is associated with a lower likelihood of achieving clinical response when compared with no treatment.

The use of prednisone in the management of CC is limited given inferior efficacy and increased side effect profile compared to budesonide.Compared to budesonide, prednisone is associated with a lower response rate, more side effects, and a higher risk of relapse when therapy is withdrawn.Bismuth subsalicylate displays anti-inflammatory action due to salicylic acid and also acts as an antacid and a mild antibiotic.A retrospective study found that most patients treated with this bismuth responded (53% complete response, 28% partial response), and that a dose of three tablets (262 mg each) three times per day appeared to be more effective than lower doses.This study also suggested that bismuth might be most effective in patients with milder degrees of diarrhea.Although based on these limited data, the use of bismuth appears to be effective and well tolerated.The use of bismuth in Western Europe is limited because it is not regularly available.For these reasons, the AGA has conditionally recommended bismuth salicylate as a second-line alternative treatment that may be appropriate for select patients who have contraindications to corticosteroids or for whom cost is a determining factor.

Cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant which binds bile in the gastrointestinal tract to prevent its reabsorption, has also been widely used for the treatment of MC, and it is considered an effective treatment in patients with MC and concomitant bile acid malabsorption (BAM).Rates of BAM and the effect of bile acid sequestration were studied in 28 patients with CC, 12 (44%) had evidence of BAM.Eleven out of these 12 patients (92%) reported improvement in diarrhea within one week when treated with bile acid binding agents (cholestyramine 4 g 2-3 times per day, or colestipol 5g 2-3 times per day if the patients could not tolerate the smell or taste of cholestyramine).Cholestyramine can be useful in patients with MC, regardless of whether there is concomitant BAM or not.

Loperamide is an opioid receptor agonist that decreases the activity of the myenteric plexus, allowing for more water to be absorbed out of the fecal matter and decreasing colonic mass movements.Although no RCTs have been performed to test its efficacy, several studies have shown clinical improvement with loperamide, but none reported sustained clinical remission.There are no RCT comparing efficacy of anti-diarrheals against placebo or other medical therapy for MC.Some authors think that anti-diarrheals may be used alone in mild MC or in conjunction with other therapies in moderate to severe MC to reduce frequency of diarrhea.

A prospective study with large cohort, with a long follow-up on the impact of dietary factors and lifestyle factors shows that, no association could be found between intake of protein, carbohydrates, different types of fat, fibre or zinc and occurrence of MC ref [23].A diet quality index based on adherence to dietary recommendations failed to reveal any differences between cases and non-cases ref [23]. The indication for surgical intervention is currently limited given the improved pharmacological treatment options.On the other hand, there are case reports of patients successfully undergoing colectomy or diverting ileostomy for refractory and severe MC.Considering advances in medical therapy the indication for surgery is limited.

Microscopic colitis is relatively common cause of chronic watery (non-bloody) diarrhoea, particularly in the female elderly population ref [16].The diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms and requires colon biopsies from many segments ref [16].There is growing need to create awareness among general practitioner, gastroenterologist, pathologist and other medical doctors to refer the patient with chronic diarrhea for a colonoscopy.It is essential for gastroenterologist and endoscopist to obtain adequate biopsies at pancolonoscopy, although the colonic mucosa is normal, and pathologist to recognize features of MC ref [16].Great number of patients are still neglected or even misdiagnosed with IBS.As far as newly identified markers hold some potential, so far, none of the tested markers present sufficient accuracy for use in clinical practice, appearing as more useful to study MC pathogenic mechanisms, rather than to predict disease activity.The ideal biomarker for MC should correspond with lymphocyte collection in the mucosal layer, the collagenous band and also distinguishing MC from either healthy subjects or other forms of IBD.At the present time MC is considered as a worldwide condition, as common as IBD ref [16].Future research should focus on a better understanding of the underlying pathophysiological and immunological mechanisms, as well as the finding of biomarkers that reflect disease activity.There is also a need for further randomized placebo-controlled studies, especially with immunomodulators and anti-TNF drugs, in order to provide better long-term therapeutic strategies and better clinical management of the patients with microscopic colitis ref [16].
